etymology: From the Old French marinier, from the Latin marinus, “of the sea” (mare, “sea”); hence a seaman, a sailor, a man whose calling and livelihood are upon the water.
biblical_def: A mariner is a seaman — the man whose trade is the deep, who handles rope and oar and sail for his bread. Scripture gives him two great appearances. In Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre he is part of the glory of a merchant empire: “the inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners: thy wise men, O Tyrus, that were in thee, were thy pilots” (Eze 27:8). And he is part of her ruin: “thy mariners, and thy pilots… shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin” (Eze 27:27), until “all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land” (Eze 27:29). The men who mastered the water stand at last on the shore with nothing. In Jonah he is a heathen sailor made to see the hand of God: “then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god” (Jon 1:5), and when at last “they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging” (Jon 1:15), those same heathen feared the LORD exceedingly, offered a sacrifice, and made vows (Jon 1:16). The Psalmist explains why the mariner is set before us at all: “they that go down to the sea in ships… these see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep” (Psa 107:23–24). No man stands nearer the naked power of God than the mariner, and no man is more tempted to credit his own hand for surviving it.
webster_summary: A seaman; a sailor; one whose occupation is to navigate ships upon the sea.
webster_full: MARINER, a seaman or sailor; one whose occupation is to assist in navigating ships.
From the Latin marinus, “of the sea,” from mare, “the sea.”
It names the working seaman, distinguished from the pilot and the shipmaster who direct him.
The AV joins mariners with pilots and calkers in the trade of Tyre (Eze 27:9, 27).
Jonah’s mariners were heathen sailors brought to fear the LORD exceedingly (Jon 1:5, 16).
scriptures: Eze 27:8
The inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners: thy wise men, O Tyrus, that were in thee, were thy pilots.
Jon 1:15
So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging.
And all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land;
Jon 1:5

Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep.
corruption_summary: A plain word for the seaman; the live misuse is the old myth of the self-sufficient man who masters the sea and needs no God upon it.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the word carries is the oldest flattery of the fallen heart: that the sea is a thing man conquers by skill. Tyre believed it. She built her ships of the fir of Senir and her masts of the cedars of Lebanon, hired the wise men of Gebal to calk her seams, filled her decks with the best mariners of the coast, and said in her heart that the deep was hers. Ezekiel answers that the whole company — mariners, pilots, calkers, men of war — goes down together in the day of her ruin. The modern version of the boast is not a merchant fleet but a technology: charts, engines, satellites, and the settled assumption that the sea has been solved. It has not been solved. The mariner sees the works of the LORD in the deep precisely because the deep will not be tamed, and every seaman who has felt a hull shudder under him knows it whatever he says on shore.

The mercy in the word is that God takes heathen mariners and makes them worshippers. Jonah’s sailors began the chapter each crying to his own god and casting the cargo overboard; they ended it fearing the LORD exceedingly, offering a sacrifice, and making vows — converted in a storm raised by the disobedience of a prophet who slept through it. That is how sovereign grace works: the LORD sends a tempest to chasten one man and gathers a shipload of Gentiles in the doing of it. The mariner is therefore not merely a figure of peril but a standing witness that no man is out of God’s reach on the widest water, and that the LORD who commands the stormy wind commands the hearts of the men He drives with it.
roots_summary: The word means a seaman — a man of the sea, from the Latin for “the sea.”
roots_lines: Mariner — Old French marinier, from Latin marinus, “of the sea.”
The root is mare, “the sea” — the same root behind marine and maritime.
In the AV he is the working seaman, ranked beside pilots and calkers (Eze 27:27).
Ezekiel drowns the whole company with the city they served (Eze 27:27, 29).
Jonah’s mariners are heathen sailors converted in the storm (Jon 1:5, 16).
usage: The mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god — and ended the chapter fearing the LORD.
A mariner sees the works of the LORD in the deep because the deep will not be mastered.
Tyre’s mariners went down with her merchandise: skill cannot outlive the judgment of God.

etymology: From ship and master; the captain of a vessel. It renders the Hebrew rab hachobel, “chief of the ropemen,” and the Greek kubernetes, “steersman, governor” — the man who commands the ship and answers for her.
biblical_def: The shipmaster is the captain — the man over the mariners, who gives the orders, holds the course, and bears the blame. The AV uses the word twice, and both times he speaks to shame somebody. In Joppa the vessel is breaking under a tempest the LORD Himself has sent, the crew are heaving the cargo over the side, and the prophet of God is asleep below: “so the shipmaster came to him, and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not” (Jon 1:6). A heathen captain must summon the prophet of the LORD to prayer. There is no sharper rebuke in the Old Testament to a minister asleep in a storm of his own making. The second use stands over the fall of the great harlot city: “every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors, and as many as trade by sea, stood afar off” (Rev 18:17), and they cast dust on their heads and cried, “Alas, alas, that great city… for in one hour is she made desolate” (Rev 18:19). The captains weep, and it is not for her sins but for their freight. In both places the shipmaster is a man of authority who finds his authority worth nothing when God moves.
webster_summary: The captain or master of a ship; the man who commands a vessel and her company.
webster_full: SHIPMASTER, the captain, master, or commander of a ship.
From ship and master; he governs the mariners and answers for the vessel.
It renders the Hebrew rab hachobel, “chief of the ropemen” (Jon 1:6).
In the Greek it is kubernetes, the steersman or governor (Rev 18:17).
The AV uses the word only twice — at Joppa and over fallen Babylon.
scriptures: Jon 1:6
So the shipmaster came to him, and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not.
Jon 1:5

Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep.
For in one hour so great riches is come to nought. And every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors, and as many as trade by sea, stood afar off,

And they cast dust on their heads, and cried, weeping and wailing, saying, Alas, alas, that great city, wherein were made rich all that had ships in the sea by reason of her costliness! for in one hour is she made desolate.
corruption_summary: The word is uncorrupted; the standing rebuke it carries is the sleeping servant of God awakened by a pagan captain.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse to name is not a redefinition of the word but a condition of the church the word exposes. Jonah is the picture of a man who has fled his commission, gone down to Joppa, gone down into the ship, gone down into the sides of the ship, and gone down into sleep — every step downward, and every step quieter. The sea is roaring, the crew is emptying the hold, and the one man aboard who knows the true God is unconscious. It takes an idolater to shake him and ask, “What meanest thou, O sleeper?” A minister, a father, an elder, a professing Christian may be that man: sound in doctrine, asleep in the storm, while the world around him works and fears and prays to gods that cannot hear. The rebuke is not that the shipmaster was too bold. It is that he had to speak at all.

The second shipmaster stands at a safe distance and weeps over a burning city, and his tears are worth nothing because they are tears for cargo. Revelation lists what the merchants and captains mourn — gold, silk, cinnamon, and last of all “slaves, and souls of men” — and the order of that list is the indictment. A trade can be lawful and a heart still be a harlot’s; the sin of these captains is that Babylon made them rich and they never once asked what she was. The principle to recover is that authority is stewardship. The shipmaster commands a vessel he did not make, on a sea he cannot govern, under a God who sinks empires in an hour; and the only captain who ends well is the one who knows whose water he sails.
roots_summary: The word means the captain of a ship — the master over her company.
roots_lines: Shipmaster — ship + master, the commander of a vessel.
Hebrew rab hachobel, literally “chief of the ropemen” (Jon 1:6).
Greek kubernetes, “steersman, governor” — root of our govern (Rev 18:17).
At Joppa a heathen captain rebukes a sleeping prophet.
Over Babylon the captains weep for their freight, not for her sin.
usage: What meanest thou, O sleeper? — a pagan captain rousing the prophet of God.
The shipmaster commands the crew but cannot command the sea.
Babylon’s shipmasters wept for lost cargo and never asked what she was.

etymology: From the Saxon rother, a paddle or steering-oar, akin to row; the blade at a vessel’s stern by which her course is governed. The AV form is rudder bands (Act 27:40) — the lashings that held the steering-oars.
biblical_def: The rudder is the steering-gear — in the ancient ship a pair of broad oars hung at the stern, worked by the helmsman, and lashed up out of the water when a vessel had to run before a gale. The AV names them only once, and at exactly the right moment. Paul’s ship has been driven for fourteen days, the tackling is gone, the anchors are down, and at daybreak they make their run for the beach: “and when they had taken up the anchors, they committed themselves unto the sea, and loosed the rudder bands, and hoised up the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore” (Act 27:40). For a fortnight the ship had no steering at all; she went where the tempest carried her. Now the lashings come off, and men take hold of the helm again. James draws the doctrine out of the same piece of timber: “behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth” (Jas 3:4). The rudder is the little thing that rules the great thing — which is why he sets it beside the tongue. And behind every helmsman stands the LORD who alone “maketh the storm a calm” (Psa 107:29).
webster_summary: The instrument at a ship’s stern by which her course is directed; the helm.
webster_full: RUDDER, the instrument by which a ship is steered; that part of the helm which enters the water.
From the Saxon rother, a paddle or oar, akin to row.
In ancient vessels it was a pair of broad steering-oars hung at the quarters.
The AV speaks of rudder bands — the lashings that secured them in a storm (Act 27:40).
James makes the small helm governing a great ship a figure of the tongue (Jas 3:4).
scriptures: And when they had taken up the anchors, they committed themselves unto the sea, and loosed the rudder bands, and hoised up the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore.
Jas 3:4
Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth.
And when neither sun nor stars in many days appeared, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope that we should be saved was then taken away.
He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still.
corruption_summary: No modern redefinition; the live error is the notion that small things do not steer a life.
corruption_paragraphs: The error the rudder rebukes is the everyday self-deceit that little things are little. A man will defend a habit on the ground that it is small: one indulgence, one hour, one word, one glance, one friendship, one omitted duty. James answers with a piece of ship’s timber a boy could lift, hung on the stern of a vessel that carried two hundred and seventy-six souls, and says that this is what turns her, fierce winds and all, wherever the governor pleases. A course is not altered by great acts; it is altered by a hand on the helm, held steadily, in a direction nobody notices for a hundred miles. The tongue steers a marriage. A morning habit steers a decade. Small does not mean weak — small means concentrated, and Scripture never once treats a besetting sin as too minor to sink a man.

The comfort is the other half of Acts 27. For fourteen days that ship had no steering: the rudders were lashed, the sun and stars were hidden, and “all hope that we should be saved was then taken away” (Act 27:20). Yet not one soul was lost, because the vessel was never in fact ungoverned — the Helmsman was simply not in the stern. The LORD who commands the stormy wind also makes the storm a calm, and the same hand that drove the ship across Adria set her on the beach of Melita where He had determined she should land. When a believer has no steerage of his own left, he is not therefore adrift. He is being steered by Another, and the day comes when the bands are loosed and he takes the helm again.
roots_summary: The word means the steering-blade of a ship — the helm that governs her course.
roots_lines: Rudder — Saxon rother, a paddle or steering-oar, akin to row.
Ancient ships were steered by two broad oars at the stern, not a single hinged blade.
Rudder bands are the lashings that hold those oars clear in heavy weather.
Loosing them (Act 27:40) means taking the helm again after running before the storm.
The Greek behind “governor” in Jas 3:4 is kubernetes, the steersman.
usage: They loosed the rudder bands and made toward shore — steerage recovered at last.
A very small helm turns a great ship: the tongue governs the whole course of a life.
Fourteen days without a rudder, and not one soul lost — the ship was never ungoverned.

etymology: From tackle, Middle Low German takel, ship’s rigging or gear; hence the ropes, blocks, spars, sails, and furniture of a vessel — everything that works her, apart from the hull itself.
biblical_def: The tackling is the ship’s gear — her cordage, blocks, spars, and spare sails, the whole apparatus by which she is worked. It is not luxury; it is the equipment of the trade. And in the AV it goes over the side. Luke keeps the log of the days precisely: on the first they lightened the ship, and “the third day we cast out with our own hands the tackling of the ship” (Act 27:19). Mark the words — with our own hands. Seamen do not throw away their rigging while any hope remains; this is the point at which men destroy the means of their own trade to buy one more day afloat. Jonah’s crew had done the same with the cargo (Jon 1:5), and Paul’s crew finished the work days later by casting out the very wheat they meant to eat (Act 27:38). Isaiah uses the same picture for the collapse of a proud enemy: “thy tacklings are loosed; they could not well strengthen their mast, they could not spread the sail” (Isa 33:23) — a ship with everything aboard and nothing working, so that even the lame carry off the spoil. Tackling is what a storm teaches a man to let go of, and what judgment strips from the man who will not.
webster_summary: The rigging and furniture of a ship — ropes, blocks, spars, and sails; her working gear.
webster_full: TACKLING, the rigging and apparatus of a ship; instruments of action; furniture, gear.
From tackle, Middle Low German takel, ship’s cordage and blocks.
It covers the ropes, spars, blocks, and spare sails by which a vessel is worked.
Paul’s crew cast it overboard with their own hands on the third day (Act 27:19).
Isaiah pictures a doomed ship with tacklings loosed and mast unstrengthened (Isa 33:23).
scriptures: And the third day we cast out with our own hands the tackling of the ship.
And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, and cast out the wheat into the sea.
Thy tacklings are loosed; they could not well strengthen their mast, they could not spread the sail: then is the prey of a great spoil divided; the lame take the prey.
Jon 1:5

Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep.
corruption_summary: A plain sea-word; the live temptation is the refusal to throw anything overboard when God sends a storm to lighten us.
corruption_paragraphs: The instructive thing about Acts 27 is the order in which the ship was emptied. First the freight, then the tackling, and at last the very wheat they meant to eat. Every stage cost something a sailor thought he could not spare, and every stage bought another day. Our age is the opposite instinct: we add. We accumulate gear, commitments, subscriptions, obligations, and opinions until the vessel rides so low that an ordinary sea comes over the rail, and then we pray for calmer water instead of a lighter hold. God frequently answers such prayers with a gale, because a man who will not lighten his ship voluntarily will lighten it eventually. What He takes is rarely what we would have chosen, and it is almost always what was sinking us.

Isaiah shows the other end of the road — the ship whose tacklings are loosed and who can neither strengthen the mast nor spread the sail, plundered so completely that even the lame carry off the spoil. That is judgment: not a storm that empties a man, but a paralysis in which everything is still aboard and nothing will answer. The principle to recover is that possessions are gear, not ballast for the soul. Christ told a whole nation to seek first the kingdom and let the rest follow; Paul counted all things loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus his Lord. A Christian holds his tackling with an open hand, ready to cast it out with his own hands if the voyage requires it, because he is not sailing for cargo. He is sailing for a haven.
roots_summary: The word means a ship’s rigging and working gear — her ropes, blocks, spars, and sails.
roots_lines: Tackling — from tackle, Middle Low German takel, ship’s gear.
It is the working apparatus of a vessel, distinct from her hull and her cargo.
Acts 27 empties the ship in three stages: freight, tackling, then the wheat itself.
“With our own hands” marks the point where seamen destroy their own trade to live.
Isaiah’s loosed tacklings picture a proud enemy fully equipped and wholly helpless (Isa 33:23).
usage: The third day we cast out with our own hands the tackling of the ship.
Tackling is what a storm teaches a man he can live without.
Thy tacklings are loosed — everything aboard, and nothing that will answer.

etymology: From under and the Saxon gyrdan, “to bind about, to encircle”; the Greek hupozonnumi. It names the seaman’s practice of passing cables beneath a labouring hull and hauling them tight, to hold her seams together in heavy weather.
biblical_def: Undergirding is frapping a ship — passing stout cables under the keel and round the hull, then hauling them taut, so that a vessel working herself apart in a gale is bound together from beneath. It is one of the most vivid words in the AV, and it comes at the crisis of Paul’s voyage: “which when they had taken up, they used helps, undergirding the ship; and, fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands, strake sail, and so were driven” (Act 27:17). Helps is the sailor’s word for expedients — whatever will serve. The ship was coming apart, and men went over the side with rope to hold her together. Here is the doctrine of means in one picture. God had already promised through Paul that there should be no loss of any man’s life; the promise did not make the cables idle, and the cables did not make the promise unnecessary. The same apostle says plainly, “except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved” (Act 27:31) — a sovereign decree and an ordinary duty in the same chapter, without apology. And underneath the timber and the rope is the older word: “the eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (Deu 33:27). Every believer who has held together in a storm has been undergirded from beneath by arms he never saw.
webster_summary: To bind a ship’s hull together with cables passed beneath her; to brace or support from underneath.
webster_full: UNDERGIRD, to bind below; to gird round the bottom, as a ship in distress.
From under and the Saxon gyrdan, “to bind about, to encircle.”
The Greek hupozonnumi names the seaman’s frapping-cables passed under the keel.
It was done to keep a labouring hull from working her seams apart in heavy weather.
The AV uses it once, at the crisis of Paul’s shipwreck (Act 27:17).
scriptures: Which when they had taken up, they used helps, undergirding the ship; and, fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands, strake sail, and so were driven.
The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms: and he shall thrust out the enemy from before thee; and shall say, Destroy them.
Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved.
Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me.
corruption_summary: The word is uncorrupted; the error it destroys is the old fatalism that sets God’s decree against the means God appoints.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors are answered by one rope. The first says: God has promised, therefore effort is unbelief — a fatalism that lets the seams open and calls it faith. The second says: the ship is ours to save, therefore let us undergird and never pray — the practical atheism of competence. Acts 27 refuses both. An angel of the God whose Paul was had stood by him in the night and said that God had given him all them that sailed with him, so that he could tell the whole company, “be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me” (Act 27:25); and the very next morning those same men were passing cables under the hull, because the God who ordains the end ordains the rope. When Paul saw the sailors trying to slip away in the boat, he did not say the promise made their presence indifferent. He said, “except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved.” The decree stood; the duty stood; and every soul came safe to land.

This is the doctrine of the means of grace in a working figure. The believer is kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, and he is kept by the Word, prayer, the Lord’s Day, the preached gospel, the Table, and the fellowship of the saints — cables God Himself passes under the hull. To despise them because election is certain is to reason like a man who will not eat because his days are numbered. And the deepest comfort lies deeper than the rope: underneath are the everlasting arms. The seamen’s cables held for a few days and the ship broke anyway; the arms beneath never gave, and every man came ashore, some on boards and some on broken pieces — not one of them lost, though the vessel that carried them was destroyed.
roots_summary: The word means to bind a straining hull together with cables passed underneath her.
roots_lines: Undergirding — under + Saxon gyrdan, “to bind about.”
Greek hupozonnumi: to pass a girdle beneath — the seaman’s frapping-cables.
“Helps” in the same verse is the sailor’s word for expedients, whatever will serve.
A KJV hapax, set at the crisis of the Adria storm (Act 27:17).
Its theological twin is underneath are the everlasting arms (Deu 33:27).
usage: They used helps, undergirding the ship — the decree of God and a rope in the same hour.
Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved: the promise never idles the means.
Underneath are the everlasting arms — the undergirding no storm has ever parted.

etymology: From quick in its old sense of “living, moving” (as in the quick and the dead) and sand; hence sand that shifts and swallows. In Act 27:17 it renders the Greek Syrtis, the dreaded shoals off the North African coast.
biblical_def: The quicksands are the shifting shoals — ground that is not ground, sand that moves under weight and takes down what rests on it. The word is quick in its old sense: living, stirring, alive. Every seaman of the ancient Mediterranean feared the great sandbanks of the African coast, where a hull could ground far from any shore and be pounded to pieces with the land nowhere in sight. That fear steers the whole narrative of Paul’s shipwreck: “fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands, strake sail, and so were driven” (Act 27:17). They lowered the gear and surrendered the ship to the wind rather than risk the sand — and being driven is what carried them across Adria for fourteen days. The same fear recurs off Melita: “then fearing lest we should have fallen upon rocks, they cast four anchors out of the stern, and wished for the day” (Act 27:29). And in the end, “when it was day, they knew not the land: but they discovered a certain creek with a shore” (Act 27:39), and the ship grounded anyway, “falling into a place where two seas met” (Act 27:41), on the ground God had appointed rather than the ground they dreaded. Men steer by their fears; God steers by His purpose. The mariners who saw all this were seeing what the Psalmist promised they would: “the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep” (Psa 107:24).
webster_summary: Shifting sand that yields under weight and swallows what rests upon it; a treacherous shoal.
webster_full: QUICKSAND, sand easily moved or readily yielding to pressure; a bank of loose sand that engulfs.
From quick in the old sense “living, moving,” as in the quick and the dead.
At sea it names a shoal where a vessel grounds and is broken far from shore.
In Act 27:17 it renders the Greek Syrtis, the shoals off the African coast.
Dread of it made Paul’s crew strike sail and let the ship be driven.
scriptures: Which when they had taken up, they used helps, undergirding the ship; and, fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands, strake sail, and so were driven.
And when it was day, they knew not the land: but they discovered a certain creek with a shore, into the which they were minded, if it were possible, to thrust in the ship.
And falling into a place where two seas met, they ran the ship aground; and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves.
These see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep.
corruption_summary: A hazard of the sea made a figure of every foundation that looks like ground and is not.
corruption_paragraphs: Our age has built its house on the quicksands and named the sand freedom. Truth is said to shift with the century, morality with the majority, and the very meaning of man and woman with the will of the one describing himself; and the whole arrangement is offered as liberation from the tyranny of fixed things. But sand that moves is not liberty, it is a shoal. A generation taught that nothing is settled cannot settle anything — not a marriage, not a conscience, not a definition — and it grounds in open water with no shore in sight. Christ set the two foundations side by side and gave the outcome without hedging: the house on the rock stood, and the house on the sand fell, and great was the fall of it. What the sailors feared as the worst death at sea is precisely what modern man has chosen to build upon.

The second lesson is quieter, and it is about fear. Twice in this chapter the crew acts out of dread — fearing the quicksands, fearing the rocks — and both times the fear is reasonable and both times it is not the thing that decides the outcome. They struck sail to avoid the Syrtis and were driven across the whole of Adria; they cast four anchors to avoid the rocks and wished for the day. In the end the ship grounded where two seas met and broke apart, and every soul walked ashore. God had already said so. The believer’s fears are seldom foolish and seldom sovereign; they steer him this way and that, while a hand he cannot see brings the vessel to the beach that was appointed before the voyage began.
roots_summary: The word means shifting sand — ground that is alive, that moves, and that swallows.
roots_lines: Quicksands — quick (“living, moving”) + sand.
The old sense of quick survives in the quick and the dead.
In Act 27:17 it renders Syrtis, the great shoals off North Africa.
Grounding there meant destruction far from any shore — the seaman’s worst end.
Fear of it, not the thing itself, drove Paul’s ship across Adria.
usage: Fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands, they strake sail, and so were driven.
Quicksand is ground that looks like ground and is not — the figure of every false foundation.
They steered by their fears; God steered by His purpose, and all came safe to land.

etymology: From the Saxon ar, an oar; a long shaft with a broad blade, worked against the side of a vessel to drive her through the water by the strength of men.
biblical_def: The oar is man’s own strength applied to the sea. It is the tool of the calm and the tool of the desperate hour, and Scripture uses it for both. Ezekiel builds Tyre’s glory out of the finest timber in the world: “of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars” (Eze 27:6); and he ends by setting the whole trade ashore in mourning: “all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land” (Eze 27:29). The men who drove the commerce of the nations stand at last on the beach with empty hands. Jonah’s crew show what the oar is worth against the purpose of God: “nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them” (Jon 1:13). They pulled with everything in them to spare a man’s life, and the sea refused, because the LORD had appointed otherwise. The disciples knew the same labour when Christ “saw them toiling in rowing; for the wind was contrary unto them” (Mar 6:48). And Isaiah promises a country where the oar is not needed at all: “wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby” (Isa 33:21) — the broad rivers of the glorious LORD, where no man rows.
webster_summary: A long shaft with a broad blade, used to row or propel a vessel through the water.
webster_full: OAR, an instrument for rowing boats; a piece of timber flat at one end and round at the other.
From the Saxon ar; it is worked against the vessel’s side to drive her forward.
Tyre’s oars were made of the oaks of Bashan — the best timber of the region (Eze 27:6).
“All that handle the oar” is the AV’s phrase for the rowing seamen (Eze 27:29).
Isaiah’s city of God has broad rivers where no galley with oars shall go (Isa 33:21).
scriptures: Eze 27:6
Of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars; the company of the Ashurites have made thy benches of ivory, brought out of the isles of Chittim.
And all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land;
Jon 1:13
Nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them.
But there the glorious LORD will be unto us a place of broad rivers and streams; wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby.
corruption_summary: A plain implement made a standing figure of human effort — honourable in its place, useless against the will of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The oar is the perfect emblem of the religion of works. It is not wicked; it is honest labour, and Scripture never sneers at it. But it has a limit, and the limit is absolute: when the sea works against a man, he may row hard and he cannot land. Jonah’s sailors are the picture. They did not want to throw the prophet over; they pulled for the shore with everything they had, and the water fought them back, because the LORD had determined that this man should go into the deep. Every attempt to save oneself by effort ends on that verse. The moralist rows hard. The religious man rows hard. The self-reformer rows hard. And the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them — for no man can bring his own vessel to land against the settled purpose of God, and the only deliverance is the one God Himself appoints.

There is honour in the oar all the same, and the gospel does not abolish labour; it re-orders it. Christ saw His own disciples toiling in rowing against a contrary wind, and He did not rebuke the rowing — He came to them on the water. The Christian pulls at his duties, his callings, his family, his mortification of sin, and pulls hard; but he pulls knowing that arrival is not the fruit of his stroke. Isaiah names the end of the matter: a place of broad rivers and streams where no galley with oars shall go, because the LORD is our judge, our lawgiver, and our king, and He will save us. Heaven has no rowing benches. The labour of the saints ceases where their salvation always rested — not on the oar, but on Him.
roots_summary: The word means the rowing-shaft by which men drive a vessel through the water.
roots_lines: Oar — Saxon ar, the rowing implement of a boat or galley.
Tyre’s were cut from the oaks of Bashan, the strongest timber of the land (Eze 27:6).
“All that handle the oar” is the AV’s name for the rowing crew (Eze 27:29).
Jonah’s mariners rowed hard and could not land — effort against decree (Jon 1:13).
In Isaiah’s city of God no galley with oars passes at all (Isa 33:21).
usage: The men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not.
All that handle the oar shall come down from their ships and stand upon the land.
No galley with oars goes on those broad rivers — heaven has no rowing benches.

etymology: From the Saxon maest, a pole or upright beam; the tall spar set upright in a vessel to carry her yard and sail — her chief timber, and the highest and most exposed place aboard.
biblical_def: The mast is the ship’s upright spar — her chief timber, the pole that carries the sail and stands highest above the deck. In Ezekiel it belongs to Tyre’s splendour: “they have taken cedars from Lebanon to make masts for thee” (Eze 27:5). In Isaiah it belongs to her enemy’s collapse: “thy tacklings are loosed; they could not well strengthen their mast, they could not spread the sail” (Isa 33:23) — a ship so helpless that even the lame carry off her spoil. But the great use is Solomon’s, and it is a portrait of the drunkard. Having asked who has woe, sorrow, contentions, and wounds without cause, he answers: they that tarry long at the wine. Then he draws the man: “yea, thou shalt be as he that lieth down in the midst of the sea, or as he that lieth upon the top of a mast” (Pro 23:34). Consider the figure. The masthead is the one place aboard where a man must be awake, and the drunkard sleeps there, reeling above the deck, insensible of a height that would sober any other man. And when he wakes: “they have stricken me… and I was not sick… when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again” (Pro 23:35). Bruised, senseless, and already reaching for the cup. That is the mast of Proverbs — the height a man cannot feel he is falling from.
webster_summary: The upright spar of a vessel, carrying her yard and sail; her chief and tallest timber.
webster_full: MAST, a long round piece of timber elevated above the deck of a ship, to which the yards and sails are fastened.
From the Saxon maest, a pole or upright beam.
Tyre’s masts were cut from the cedars of Lebanon (Eze 27:5).
Isaiah’s doomed ship cannot well strengthen her mast nor spread her sail (Isa 33:23).
Solomon sets the drunkard asleep upon the top of a mast (Pro 23:34).
scriptures: Yea, thou shalt be as he that lieth down in the midst of the sea, or as he that lieth upon the top of a mast.
They have stricken me, shalt thou say, and I was not sick; they have beaten me, and I felt it not: when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again.
Thy tacklings are loosed; they could not well strengthen their mast, they could not spread the sail: then is the prey of a great spoil divided; the lame take the prey.
Eze 27:5
They have made all thy ship boards of fir trees of Senir: they have taken cedars from Lebanon to make masts for thee.
corruption_summary: The mast itself is uncorrupted; the corruption is our age’s refusal to believe that the man asleep at the masthead is in any danger.
corruption_paragraphs: Solomon’s figure is the sharpest description of insensibility in Scripture, and it is aimed at a sin our age has domesticated. The drunkard is not merely in danger; he cannot feel the danger. He lies at the top of a mast, swaying over open water, and sleeps. He is struck and does not know it, beaten and does not feel it, and his first waking thought is where to get more. The modern arrangement calls this a coping mechanism and treats the numbness as the treatment; Scripture calls the numbness the disease. What makes the masthead deadly is not the height but the sleep. A man who could feel where he was would climb down. The mercy God often sends is therefore a hard one — He lets a man feel the blow he had been anaesthetising, because a drunkard who hurts is a drunkard who might come home.

The mast is also, in its proper use, a picture of what men build to be seen. Tyre cut hers from the cedars of Lebanon, the finest timber in the world, and Isaiah’s ruined vessel could not strengthen hers at all. A mast is height and visibility and reach — and it is exactly what fails first when God withdraws His hand, leaving a ship fully rigged and unable to spread a sail, plundered by the lame. The principle to recover is sobriety in its full biblical breadth: not merely abstinence from the cup but a waking, watching, self-possessed mind, the mind Peter commands when he says be sober, be vigilant. The Christian is a man awake at the masthead, and his sobriety is not the enemy of his joy but the condition of it.
roots_summary: The word means the upright spar of a ship — her tallest timber and her most exposed place.
roots_lines: Mast — Saxon maest, a pole or upright beam.
It carries the yard and sail and stands highest above the deck.
Tyre’s masts came from the cedars of Lebanon, her boards from the fir of Senir (Eze 27:5).
A ship that cannot strengthen her mast cannot spread her sail (Isa 33:23).
Proverbs sets the drunkard asleep at the masthead — peril without sensation (Pro 23:34).
usage: As he that lieth upon the top of a mast — the drunkard asleep where no man dare sleep.
They could not well strengthen their mast: a ship fully rigged and wholly helpless.
The Christian is a man awake at the masthead, sober because he is watching.

etymology: From the Saxon haefen, a harbour, akin to have and hold — a place that holds; hence a sheltered anchorage where a ship rides safe out of the reach of the sea.
biblical_def: A haven is a harbour — the sheltered water where a vessel lies at rest, held safe from the sea that has been beating her. The word is a place of arrival, and Scripture makes it a place of doctrine. Zebulun’s inheritance is described by it: “Zebulun shall dwell at the haven of the sea; and he shall be for an haven of ships” (Gen 49:13). But the great haven of the AV is the last line of the seafarer’s psalm. The Psalmist has taken us out with the merchants: “they that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters” (Psa 107:23); he has raised the stormy wind that lifts up the waves and reeled them to and fro like a drunken man till they are at their wits’ end; he has heard them cry unto the LORD in their trouble; and then, “he maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still” (Psa 107:29). And then the line that ends the voyage: “then are they glad because they be quiet; so he bringeth them unto their desired haven” (Psa 107:30). Mark that the calm is not the haven. The calm is a mercy granted on the passage; the haven is the end of the passage. The believer’s desired haven is glory — the harbour where the voyage is over, the ship is moored, and there is no more sea.
webster_summary: A harbour or port; a sheltered anchorage where ships ride safe; hence a place of rest and refuge.
webster_full: HAVEN, a harbor; a port; a bay or inlet where ships can ride secure from storms.
From the Saxon haefen, akin to have and hold — a place that holds.
By extension, any shelter, asylum, or place of safety and rest.
Zebulun’s border is described as the haven of the sea and a haven of ships (Gen 49:13).
Psa 107:30 makes the desired haven the end of the storm-tossed voyage.
scriptures: Then are they glad because they be quiet; so he bringeth them unto their desired haven.
They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters;
He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still.
Zebulun shall dwell at the haven of the sea; and he shall be for an haven of ships; and his border shall be unto Zidon.
corruption_summary: The corruption is not of the word but of its address: our age seeks the desired haven on this side of the grave and calls every calm an arrival.
corruption_paragraphs: Men will have a haven; the only question is where they look for it. The age offers several, all of them anchorages in open water: the retirement that will finally settle everything, the house that will make a family whole, the salary at which anxiety stops, the relationship that ends loneliness, the therapy that closes the old wound for good. Each is offered as harbour and each is a roadstead — sheltered enough to feel like arrival, open enough that the next gale finds you there. Scripture is not cruel about this; the Psalm grants real calms. He does make the storm a calm, and the waves are genuinely still, and the men are genuinely glad. But the psalm does not stop there, and neither should we. A calm is a mercy in the passage. It is not the port.

The desired haven is glorification. Every voyage in this life ends short of it: the believer is brought through storm after storm, quieted, blown out again, quieted again, and every deliverance is a foretaste and none of them is the harbour. The harbour is the LORD Himself, entered at the end — where the sea that has tossed the church since Eden is gone, where John saw the new heaven and the new earth and recorded that there was no more sea. This is why the Christian can lose the calm and keep his gladness. His hope is an anchor of the soul, sure and stedfast, already cast within the veil where his Forerunner is entered; the mooring is fast in the haven before the ship is. He is not sailing hopefully toward a port that may not be there. He is being brought to a haven already prepared, by a Pilot who has never lost a vessel.
roots_summary: The word means a harbour — the sheltered water that holds a ship safe at the end of her voyage.
roots_lines: Haven — Saxon haefen, a harbour, akin to have and hold.
The root idea is a place that holds — shelter that keeps what enters it.
By extension it means any refuge, asylum, or place of rest.
Gen 49:13 uses it geographically of Zebulun’s coastal inheritance.
Psa 107:30 uses it doctrinally: the desired haven at the voyage’s end.
usage: So he bringeth them unto their desired haven — the end of the voyage, not a lull in it.
He maketh the storm a calm: the calm is a mercy on the passage, the haven is the port.
The believer’s haven is glory, where the sea that tossed the church is no more.

etymology: From east and wind, rendering the Hebrew qadim, the wind from the eastern quarter. In Palestine it blows off the desert — scorching, dry, and violent — and in Scripture it is always in the hand of God.
biblical_def: The east wind is the desert wind — hot, dry, withering, and in the AV never a bare fact of weather. It is an instrument, and the LORD wields it. It brings judgment upon Egypt: “the LORD brought an east wind upon the land all that day, and all that night; and when it was morning, the east wind brought the locusts” (Exo 10:13). It blasts the grain of Pharaoh’s dream: “behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them” (Gen 41:6), and seven years of famine follow. It chastens a sulking prophet outside Nineveh: “God prepared a vehement east wind; and the sun beat upon the head of Jonah, that he fainted” (Jon 4:8) — the same verb of divine preparing that appointed the fish, the gourd, and the worm. It breaks the ships of Tarshish (Psa 48:7) and dries up the fountain of a fruitful man (Hos 13:15). And then, at the Red Sea, the identical wind opens the road of salvation: “the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided” (Exo 14:21). One wind, one hand. It scourges Egypt and it delivers Israel in the same book. The east wind is the whole doctrine of providence blowing off a desert.
webster_summary: The scorching desert wind from the east; in Scripture, God’s appointed instrument of blasting and of deliverance.
webster_full: EAST WIND, the wind that blows from the east; in the Levant, a dry and burning wind off the desert.
It renders the Hebrew qadim, the wind of the eastern quarter.
It withers grain, dries springs, and breaks ships (Gen 41:6; Hos 13:15; Psa 48:7).
God brought it upon Egypt to carry in the locusts (Exo 10:13).
By a strong east wind He divided the Red Sea for Israel (Exo 14:21).
scriptures: And Moses stretched forth his rod over the land of Egypt, and the LORD brought an east wind upon the land all that day, and all that night; and when it was morning, the east wind brought the locusts.
And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea; and the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.
Jon 4:8

And it came to pass, when the sun did arise, that God prepared a vehement east wind; and the sun beat upon the head of Jonah, that he fainted, and wished in himself to die, and said, It is better for me to die than to live.
Gen 41:6
And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them.
corruption_summary: The standing corruption is naturalism — treating the east wind as mere meteorology and reading God out of His own miracles.
corruption_paragraphs: The east wind is the favourite handle of those who wish to keep the Bible’s stories and lose the Bible’s God. Because Exo 14:21 names a strong east wind, it is confidently explained that the Red Sea was a wind-driven tide over a shallow marsh, a natural event that Israel afterwards dressed up as a miracle. The text will not carry it. The waters stood as a wall on the right hand and on the left; the sea returned to his strength and drowned the whole host of Pharaoh; and the same LORD who is credited with sending the wind is the one whose hand Moses stretched out. Naming the second cause never removes the First. Scripture is entirely comfortable saying that God did it and that a wind did it, because the wind is His and blows at His word. The corruption is not in the wind; it is in the assumption that any event with a mechanism has no Author.

The doctrine to recover is the sovereignty of God over the ordinary weather of a life. One wind carried the locusts that broke Egypt and one wind opened the road out of Egypt, and it was the same wind from the same hand for the same purpose — the glory of the LORD and the salvation of His people. Jonah’s east wind was prepared as deliberately as the great fish, and it was not sent to kill him but to break a heart that had pitied a gourd and would not pity a city. So the believer learns to read his own hard weather. The wind that withers your gourd is prepared. The wind that dries your fountain is prepared. And the wind that seems set to destroy you is quite possibly the very wind that is dividing a sea in front of you, though you will not see the dry ground until the morning watch.
roots_summary: The word names the scorching desert wind — God’s instrument of both chastening and deliverance.
roots_lines: East wind — Hebrew qadim, the wind from the eastern quarter.
In Palestine it blows off the desert: hot, dry, and violent.
It blasts grain (Gen 41:6), dries springs (Hos 13:15), and breaks ships (Psa 48:7).
It carried the locusts into Egypt in the eighth plague (Exo 10:13).
It divided the Red Sea and made a road for Israel (Exo 14:21).
usage: The east wind brought the locusts — judgment arriving on an ordinary breeze.
God prepared a vehement east wind: even the weather over Jonah was appointed.
By a strong east wind He divided the sea — the same wind that scourged Egypt saved Israel.
